options.readme_translation: One SVG window above the fold. Rows are the project's own parts: packages, modules or milestone items, each with its true size and a bar showing something real (test coverage, milestone completion, documentation coverage). 'Sources' becomes contributors per module; the chunk map becomes a strip with one segment per test or per file, coloured passed, failing, running and missing. The lower pane lists what the project 'uploads': releases with download counts. The status bar carries stars, forks and total downloads in the 'users online, files shared' slot. Three presets select the generation: single-bar, chunk-map, or seeds-and-ratio.
options.feasibility_notes: Everything is rectangles and small text: a grid with header cells, one rect per bar with an animated width, and for the chunk map a row of 40 to 100 thin rects with staggered fill keyframes. The work is in the amount of small text and keeping it legible at README width (keep to five or six columns and four to six rows). Generic window chrome can be borrowed from the existing Windows 95/98 style.
options.caveats: Use no client name, logo or mascot, and none of the toolbar icons; the grid, bar and status-bar arrangement is generic. Rows must be the project's own files with no media-style file names, no tracker or server names and no real user names, so the header cannot look like a list of pirated downloads. The screenshots are of particular versions (eMule 0.50a, uTorrent 1.8.3 in Spanish, a Mac build of Azureus), so column sets varied by version. Small grey text on white needs care for contrast, and the eMule colour code relies on hue alone, so add a text percentage.

options.name: 16-bit hand-pixelled chrome logo (static)
options.era: 1988-1993, Amiga and Atari ST; drawn in Deluxe Paint at 320 pixels wide with 16 or 32 colours
options.what_it_is: The group logo as a piece of pixel art: metal letters reflecting an imaginary sky and desert, drawn dot by dot. Damien Guard's article on Amiga lettering describes the chrome, gradient and lens-flare conventions within 16 or 32 colours, and the book 'Demoscene: The Logo Art' is devoted to logos and their makers. Named hands exist: Demozoo credits Uno with the red and blue logos and charsets in Phenomena's 'Enigma' (1991), and the Amiga Graphics Archive documents a TRSi logo by J.O.E. in 32 colours, 19 used.
visual_signature: Chrome fill split by a horizon about halfway up each letter: cool colours above (violet or deep blue to pale blue to white), a hard zigzag line, warm colours below (dark red to orange to yellow, or grey)
Banded, stepped gradients of 5-8 colours, because the whole logo shares a 16- or 32-colour palette
A one-pixel dark outline around every letter, often with a lighter inner edge to fake a bevel
A solid drop shadow or extruded side offset down and to the right
Heavy italic or slab capitals, letters touching or overlapping
Single-hue variant (Enigma): hot red to pink letters cut by thin horizontal slits with white streak highlights, beside a violet chrome wordmark with a white horizon
Composite title variant (Red Sector Megademo): a second word set vertically beside the main logo, plus a cartoon head with a speech bubble
Chrome with white sparkle stars on letter corners over a blue gradient floor (Kefrens 'Multi Megamix' title)
options.palette: One cool ramp and one warm ramp plus black and white. Amiga colours are 12-bit, so each ramp step is one sixteenth per channel. On the ST the palette is 512 colours with 16 on screen, so ramps are shorter and coarser.
options.typography: Custom-drawn capitals only: wide letterforms with flat tops to give room for the horizon band, light from the upper left, highlights as one-pixel white lines along top edges, sparing checkerboard dither where two bands meet.
options.motion: Static as an image. An optional glint can travel across the letters.

references.what: Red Sector Megademo title (1989): violet top, zigzag horizon, orange-red base, vertical second word
Kefrens Megademo 8 menu logo (1990): blue to white to grey banded chrome
Enigma by Phenomena on Demozoo (30 March 1991): Uno credited for the red Enigma logo, blue logo and charsets; Imbecille for a logo; Terminator for charsets
Enigma on Pouet: stills of the red slit logo and the violet chrome wordmark
Amiga Graphics Archive: TRSi logo by J.O.E., used in TRSi's 'Time Zone' demo; lowres PAL, 32 colours, 19 used

Damien Guard, 'The Art of Amiga Lettering' (December 2025): chrome, gradients, lens flares and extrusion within 16 or 32 colours; mostly game titles, with Fairlight, Scoopex, The Silents and Enigma as demo examples
'Demoscene: The Logo Art' (Editions64K, 400 pages): logos and their makers across Amiga, Atari, C64, Amstrad, PC and consoles
Fairfax interview (Hugi 35): names Uno first among favourite graphicians for his use of colour and light within Amiga limits
Amiga Graphics Archive page for Cougar: several pictures credited as based on album-cover art, evidence for the caveat about adapted sources

options.readme_translation: Above the fold: a static SVG of the project name as a chrome pixel logo on black, 640-800 pixels wide, optionally with a one-line subtitle in small pixel capitals. It can stand alone or sit on top of any animated style in this family.
options.feasibility_notes: Draw letters as pixel-grid rects (run-length merged) with shape-rendering: crispEdges at 2x or 3x. Fill through a clipPath with a linearGradient that uses paired hard stops for bands; add the zigzag horizon as a polyline clipped to the letters. Dither between bands with a 2x2 checkerboard pattern. Outline and shadow are offset copies of the letter shape. Sparkles are small 4-point polygons. An optional glint is a narrow skewed white rect animated across the clip. The SVG is simple; convincing letterforms are not, and a generated logo will look mechanical beside a hand-pixelled one.
options.caveats: Do not copy any existing group logo, the Red Sector head, or an artist's specific letterforms; the chrome recipe is common property. Artist attributions are only those stated by Demozoo and the Amiga Graphics Archive; which logo Imbecille drew in Enigma is not specified. Scene graphics of the period were often adapted from album covers and commercial art, another reason to draw from scratch. The brief also asked about 'graffiti' logos and other named logo artists; I could not source that school and have not described it.

options.name: LSDj phrase screen (Game Boy tracker), with the nanoloop grid as its minimalist opposite
options.era: 2000 onward, Nintendo Game Boy: Little Sound Dj by Johan Kotlinski (project dated to 2000 by the Battle of the Bits lyceum; still updated per its changelog). nanoloop by Oliver Wittchow: a study project at the University of Fine Arts Hamburg, first performed publicly in early 1998, cartridges sold in Germany from late 1999 and worldwide from 2000.
options.what_it_is: The program that made the Game Boy the standard instrument of the 2000s chiptune scene. It squeezes a whole tracker into 160x144 pixels by splitting it into screens (Song, Chain, Phrase, Instrument, Table and more) arranged on a small map. For many people this grid of three-letter codes is what 'chiptune' looks like; nanoloop answers it with almost nothing on screen but a 4x4 grid of squares.
visual_signature: A 160x144 screen of 8x8 tiles: 20 characters wide, 18 rows tall, drawn at integer scale
Screen title and hex index at top-left (PHRASE 00, SONG, WAVE 00), current channel name at top-right (WAV, PU1)
Sixteen rows numbered 0-F down the left edge in white digits on a pale pink band
Song screen: four columns headed PU1, PU2, WAV, NOI holding 2-digit hex chain numbers, double dashes where empty

Phrase screen: tiny column headers NOTE, INSTR, CMD; notes as C-3 style or, in drum-kit mode, two 3-letter drum names side by side; instruments as I00; commands as a letter plus two hex digits or ---; alternate columns banded in pale cyan
Right-hand status column: tempo with a note glyph (such as 128), the four mute letters 1 2 W N stacked vertically, a tiny squiggle waveform
Bottom-right screen map: a cross of single letters (S C P I T in a row with G above and another letter below) with the current screen's letter highlighted
A solid red-pink block cursor with white text inside, and a small black triangle at the left marking the play row
options.palette: Official phrase screenshot (a Game Boy Color palette, researcher-sampled and consistent with the image): field white #FFFFFF, column bands pale cyan #D9FBFD, text black #000000, row-number band pale pink #F8C8FA, cursor red-pink #F4788E. The Song screen photographed on a Game Boy Advance is white text on royal blue with orange row numbers and an orange map. LSDj palettes are user-selectable, so no single scheme is canonical; four greys or four greens give the original-hardware feel. nanoloop on an original Game Boy: dark olive squares on the pea-green LCD.
options.typography: One heavy 8x8 upper-case bitmap face for everything, hex digits throughout, with column headers in a much smaller face about 5 pixels tall. No lower case. nanoloop's later versions use a thin lower-case pixel face and single letters in grid cells.
options.motion: The play-row triangle steps down the 16 rows and wraps; the cursor block blinks; optionally the map highlight moves and the grid swaps to another screen. All stepped, no easing, to keep the LCD feel.

references.what: Official Little Sound Dj site (describes it as a Game Boy music sequencer; hosts the two screenshots)
Official phrase-screen screenshot at native 160x144
Photograph of the LSDj Song screen (PU1 PU2 WAV NOI, tempo, mute letters, screen map) on a Game Boy Advance
Battle of the Bits lyceum: LSDj (Johan Kotlinski, begun 2000, song / chain / phrase / instrument views, four channels)
nanoloop history from its author: Hamburg study project, first performance early 1998, cartridges from late 1999
nanoloop one running on an original Game Boy: the 4x4 grid of squares on the green LCD
CDM on nanoloop: 'minimal elements onscreen' versus LSDj's '90s-style tracker interface'
nanoloop mobile-version screen: grey field, white squares, 4x4 note grid, thin lower-case pixel lettering

options.readme_translation: One SVG with two or three 160x144 screens side by side at 3x (each 480x432) or one at 4x (640x576): SONG (the four columns renamed to the project's four modules, rows = releases), PHRASE (NOTE = command, INSTR = module id, CMD = flag) and a PROJECT-style screen (name, version, tempo = build time). The corner screen map becomes a miniature table of contents whose letters are the README sections; the real section links go in text under the image. The nanoloop variant is the opposite extreme: a bare 4x4 grid with a few lit cells and one line of type for the project name.
options.feasibility_notes: Only 360 tiles per screen. Define an original 8x8 glyph set as paths once and place with use: three screens are about 700 placements, 25-35 KB. Use shape-rendering: crispEdges and integer scale so pixels stay square. Animation is three small steps() keyframe sets (cursor blink via opacity, play-row marker via translateY with steps(16), map highlight). An LCD look is cheap: a 1px grid from an SVG pattern at low opacity, or a slight green tint.
options.caveats: Do not draw a Game Boy shell, the Nintendo or Game Boy wordmarks, the LSDj name or its font bitmaps: build an original 8x8 face and an original screen title. The 16-row hex grid, the channel abbreviations as hardware terms and the screen-map idea are reusable. Pale pastel bands are low contrast, so keep text pure black on them. Unconfirmed: LSDj's exact first-release date (2000 comes from the lyceum, not the official site; there is no English Wikipedia article for it); whether nanoloop was begun in 1997 (the author's page documents the 1998 performance only); the CDM article itself does not describe the 4x4 grid, which is confirmed from the two images instead.

options.name: Trainer menu: F-key toggles under a logo
options.era: 1993-2006: DOS trainers by Razor 1911 (1993-94); Windows trainers by Hoodlum (2004-05), Deviance (2005), FANAiON with Titan (2005) and Razor (2006)
options.what_it_is: A trainer patches a running game to give cheats, and its screen is a cracktro with a job to do: a logo on top and a list of function-key toggles underneath. It is the most list-shaped screen in the family, which makes it the easiest to turn into something useful, and the VU bars in the 1993 Razor one are the natural visual stand-in for the music a README cannot play.
visual_signature: A logo at the top, smaller than in a cracktro: a wordmark whose letters each carry a different rainbow gradient (Razor 1993, logo by Pal per Demozoo), a green-and-yellow graffiti piece (Hoodlum 2005), a grey-teal stone-textured logo (Razor Gothic 3, 2006)
A title block: 'presents', the game name with a '+N' option count, 'trained by' and the author
The list: one row per function key, key name at the left, effect at the right, sometimes ending in a bracketed [OFF] state (Razor Gothic 3)
A full-width magenta highlight bar on the selected row (Razor Alien Breed +11)
Two stubby yellow VU-meter bars in the bottom corners (same trainer)
An instruction line at the bottom saying which keys work in-game and how to continue

Windows-era additions around the centred list: a faceted green polyhedron (Hoodlum #3), a pink vector star drifting on a purple-to-blue gradient (Deviance, Hoodlum Bugdom 2), a sine scroller, or the group name spelled in shaded dots (FANAiON)
options.palette: Black background in most. Razor 1993: rainbow logo, white list, magenta bar, yellow meters. Hoodlum 2005: acid green and yellow logo, white list. Deviance 2005 and FANAiON 2005: purple-to-blue gradient field with white text and pink accents. Razor's 1994 Pinball Fantasies trainer is just a dark-red serif logo over grey text.
options.typography: Monospaced bitmap capitals so the key column and the description column align; fixed tabs or leader dots between them. Logos are custom.
options.motion: The highlight bar steps from row to row; VU bars jump; logo colours cycle; in the later ones a scroller runs under the list and the side object rotates (a commenter on Hoodlum's notes parallax stars, a rotating vector star and a sine scroll).

references.what: Razor Trainer Alien Breed +11 on Pouet (Nov 1993): rainbow logo, F-key list, magenta bar, yellow VU bars
Same on Demozoo: 4 Nov 1993; menu code Lithium, logo Pal, font Poise, trainer Red Wizard

options.readme_translation: The list is the README's feature or command table. Above the fold: a small SVG with the logo, colour cycling and VU bars; then a text-only <pre> block, for example (my own illustration): 'F1  WATCH MODE ............ [ON ]' / 'F2  DRY RUN ............... [OFF]' / 'F3  VERBOSE LOGS .......... [ON ]', each key mapping to a CLI flag or feature, with links on the descriptions. A '+7' after the project name gives the feature count.
options.feasibility_notes: The list works as plain monospace text in a code block (links work inside <pre>), so the essential part needs no SVG. Animated version in one SVG: a highlight rect stepping down the rows with steps() timing, a few rects on scaleY keyframes with different durations for VU bars, a per-letter gradient logo whose stops are keyframed. Under 10 KB.
options.caveats: Do not reuse any group logo or name. The F-key list is generic. Replace cheat wording with the project's own features and avoid implying the README does anything to other software. If ON/OFF states are shown, make them match real defaults or label them as decoration. Commenters note the Deviance trainer borrowed its font and tune from another group's work without credit: a reminder to credit sources.

options.name: C64 one-screen crack intro: raster-split logo and text on colour bars
options.era: 1986-1989, Commodore 64 cracking scene (Europe, plus NTSC intros from the US such as Eagle Soft); small intros placed in front of cracked games
options.what_it_is: The single-screen C64 intro: a group logo at the top, a few centred lines naming the game, cracker and date, and a scroller, all on black. Commenters on the C64 intro database call the Fairlight one "one of the most used intros ever" and the Eagle Soft one "THE C64-intro". It differs from the existing C64 boot/loader style: no BASIC screen and no loading stripes, only the intro itself.
visual_signature: Pure black screen and border, everything centred on a 40-column grid
Logo as one flat shape whose colour changes in horizontal bands by scanline: Dynamic Duo's two-row logo in red/green/yellow/blue bands; Ikari's upright slab capitals in blue and yellow bands
Logo drawn as an outline over a block of raster stripes: Fairlight's thin pink outlined letters sit on green/white stripes between two red rules
Logo as a mosaic of small bevelled squares: Triad's grey block-grid letters, about 6 character rows high, with one block blinking
Full-width raster bars about 8 pixels tall behind single text lines, shaded in 3-5 luminance steps (Fairlight: a pink bar behind the game title, a blue bar behind the 'CRACKED ... BY ...' line)
Fixed text block in 8x8 capitals: 'PRESENTS', game title, 'CRACKED ON dd/mm/yy BY handle', often fenced with dashes or dollar signs
One scroller near the bottom in double-width characters, plus optional 'PRESS SPACE'

Variants: brick-textured block letters on a blue panel above an orange brick wall panel with big yellow letters (Hotline); a multicolour bitmap picture panel in place of the logo with one grey label bar and a scroller under it (Eagle Soft)
options.palette: The 16 fixed VIC-II colours on black. Pepto's measured values: black 000000, white FFFFFF, red 68372B, cyan 70A4B2, purple 6F3D86, green 588D43, blue 352879, yellow B8C76F, orange 6F4F25, brown 433900, light red 9A6759, dark grey 444444, grey 6C6C6C, light green 9AD284, light blue 6C5EB5, light grey 959595. Colours share luminance levels (blue = brown, red = dark grey, purple = orange, light blue = grey, green = light red, cyan = light grey, yellow = light green), so bar shading and fades run in ramps such as blue, light blue, cyan, white or brown, orange, yellow, white.
options.typography: 8x8-pixel uppercase character sets, the ROM font or a redrawn one (thin 'computer' capitals, slab capitals). Logos are character mosaics or sprites doubled in X and Y, so edges step in 8-pixel or 2-pixel units. Scroller fonts are 1x1, 1x2 or 2x2 characters. Almost no lower case.
options.motion: Raster colours roll vertically through the logo and the text bars; the scroller moves right to left at constant speed; one element may blink. Everything else is static. Motion is taken from user comments (colour rotation on Dynamic Duo, the logo blink on Triad); only stills were viewed.

Pepto's 2001 palette page: the hex values quoted above

options.readme_translation: Above the fold: one animated SVG about 640x240 (2x scale of 320x120). Project name as the block logo with rolling raster bands, then PRESENTS, a one-line description on a raster bar, and a 'CRACKED ON' style line reused for version and date. The scroller carries the tagline or stats. Real links go in normal Markdown directly under the image.
options.feasibility_notes: Build the logo from rects on an 8-pixel grid and use it as a clipPath over a tall stack of palette-coloured stripes that translates vertically in a CSS @keyframes loop with steps() timing; that is the raster split. Text bars are rects whose fill steps through 4-5 palette colours. The scroller is one group translated on X with the text duplicated for a seamless loop. No font can load, so define the 8x8 glyphs once as symbol elements and place them with use; about 60 glyphs costs a few KB. shape-rendering: crispEdges keeps the pixels hard.
options.caveats: Do not copy any group name, logo shape or the Eagle Soft picture; the layout, raster split and block-letter technique are generic. Period scrolltexts often contain slurs (the Fairlight still shows one), so write new text. Dates are those shown on the intro screens and were not cross-checked on CSDb. Partly overlaps the 'SID title screen' part of the existing C64 style; keep this one strictly to the crack-intro layout.
